transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Laura Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (VertexWare - Head of ML), Eric Gomez (Infra), Nina Park (Product)

Summary (auto): Discovery focused on latency & throughput targets, p95 SLAs, concurrency needs, streaming behavior, and tokens/sec benchmarking. Action items and next steps captured.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros — I'm Samir, AE at Redwood. Laura's our SE, she'll jump into the perf details.
[00:14] Maya: Hi all, Maya here. We're trying to understand if Redwood Hosted or Dedicated makes sense for VertexWare's real-time assistant product. Latency is the big one for us.
[00:22] Samir: Great, do you want to start with the production targets — p95, concurrency, payload sizes?
[00:30] Maya: Sure. Our defenders — sorry, our end-users expect near instant replies. We're targeting p95 under 500ms for first token ideally, but more realistically 800ms for typical full-turns. Concurrency: peaks of ~60 concurrent users generating streaming responses, plus batch jobs overnight.
[00:45] Eric: And to add, we have bursts up to 150 concurrent open sessions during demos. We measure tokens/sec in the backbench, we need sustained throughput for embeddings and reranks too.
[00:58] Laura: Ok, couple clarifying q's — when you say p95 under 500ms, is that first token latency or full response? And what's your average response length in tokens?
[01:07] Maya: First token for interactive flows. Typical responses are 40-120 tokens. Some longer generative flows go to 600+ tokens but those are lower priority.
[01:20] Samir: Helpful. On Redwood side, hosted vs dedicated differences: Hosted optimizes for multi-tenant capacity and cost; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput. For first token p95 with small responses (<=128 tokens), we've seen p95s in the 200-400ms range on certain model configs with our optimized runtime.
[01:36] Nina: Are those numbers for streaming? Our UX relies on streaming token-by-token, we can't wait for full bufferization.
[01:42] Laura: Yes, that's streaming first-token latency. There's occasionally noisy transcription around brand names — our runtime uses continuous batching and KV cache, which helps when you have repeated prefixes in a session. For streaming throughput, token/sec depends on model size and hardware; e.g., on an A100-type GPU we can reach several hundred tokens/sec for medium-sized models, higher for smaller ones.
[02:05] Eric: We're very GPU cost-sensitive. If Dedicated, what's the expected tokens/sec per GPU and how many GPUs to reserve for our 60 concurrent streaming users?
[02:15] Laura: Ballpark numbers: for a gpt-medium-ish open model ~7B on an A100, you might see 200-400 tokens/sec per GPU for generation when running single-streaming sessions. For larger models like 13B quantized on similar hardware, maybe 80-200 tok/s. These are workload-dependent. For 60 concurrent users producing ~50 tok/s each (that's 3k tok/s), you'd want roughly 8-15 GPUs depending on batching and sequence lengths. We'll validate with your prompts.
[02:44] Maya: That math helps. What about p95 under load — like 60 concurrent plus background batch? We can't have p95 spikes to multiple seconds.
[02:53] Laura: Right. We recommend planning for p95 SLOs with headroom — autoscaling plus burst capacity. For Dedicated we can set reserved throughput targets and have fallback to hosted capacity if you need bursts. Also smart routing by policy so latency-sensitive traffic hits low-latency nodes. In practice, with aggressive KV caching for repeated prefixes and short sequences, we've hit p95s under 500ms for our customers.
[03:17] Eric: Does Redwood support streaming backpressure? If the model is slower, can we get partial tokens sooner?
[03:23] Laura: Yes, streaming is available. We stream tokens as they're generated. There's tradeoffs with batching: bigger batches increase tokens/sec efficiency but add some latency. Our runtime can do micro-batching to balance it.
[03:33] Maya: How do you measure p95? From API entry to first token at the client, or backend-only? We need E2E from our webclient to be under target.
[03:43] Samir: We report a few metrics: server-side generation latency (first token, last token), network transit times, and end-to-end as seen by SDK if you run our client libs. For hosted customers we provide dashboards with token-level breakdowns and p95 traces.
[03:56] Nina: Any example dashboards we can see?
[03:59] Laura: I'll share a benchmark spreadsheet and a couple of recent p95 dashboards. We'll redact customer names. It shows first-token p50/p95/p99 and throughput (tokens/sec) per GPU.
[04:10] Maya: Sounds good. About model variants: we need fallback to a lower-cost model if capacity is limited. How seamless is that?
[04:18] Samir: We have routing policies and automatic fallback to compatible model variants. You can define policies (e.g., if latency > 700ms or queue > X, fall back to a smaller quantized model). This keeps the app responsive.
[04:29] Eric: For Dedicated sizing, we need concrete bench numbers with our prompts. Can Redwood run a tokens/sec benchmark with our prompt set?
[04:36] Laura: Yes — ideally you give us the representative prompts, sequences length distribution, and expected concurrency. We'll run a workload test on Dedicated-like hardware and share per-GPU tokens/sec and p95.
[04:47] Maya: Ok action. We'll send prompts.
[04:50] (brief cross talk)
[05:02] Eric: Quick Q on data residency and Private deploy — we have some regulated customers. If we go Private, how different is the latency story?
[05:10] Laura: Private (VPC) can be identical from latency perspective as Dedicated if it runs on the same hardware. The difference is network topology — if you host in your VPC on-prem, network overhead and firewalls can add ms. We do support on-prem packages as well. For strict regs, Private+KMS/HSM and audit logs are available.
[05:29] Maya: And security — SOC2, SSO, RBAC?
[05:32] Samir: We have SOC 2, SSO (SAML/Okta), RBAC, audit logging and KMS integrations. We'll share our security pack.
[05:40] Nina: About noise in transcription — you said continuous batching. How do you ensure p95s don't oscillate wildly during traffic spikes?
[05:49] Laura: Continuous batching is workload-aware and we tune max-batch windows. For latency-sensitive routes we use dedicated pools or low-latency knobs that reduce batch windows and bind requests to warm KV caches. Also autoscaling and burst pools help smooth noisy spikes.
[06:05] Maya: Hypothetical: if we need p95 < 300ms for first token with 50 concurrent low-latency users, what would you recommend — Hosted, Dedicated, or Private?
[06:13] Laura: For strict sub-300ms p95 at scale, Dedicated with reserved low-latency nodes is safest. Hosted can reach there for smaller scales but it's multi-tenant so you may see more variance; Private on-prem can also if you control hardware and network.
[06:25] Eric: Do you have examples of customers with similar SLOs?
[06:29] Samir: Yes, we have a couple of real-time chat customers and a telematics vendor where p95 targets were ~300-600ms and we used Dedicated with autoscale buffers. We'll share anonymized traces.
[06:39] Maya: Ok, drilling into concurrency math — say our 60 users, average 80 tokens per response, 5 responses per minute per user during a peak, and streaming on. That roughly equates to X tok/s. Curious if Redwood recommends batching for streaming-heavy workloads or sticking to micro-batches.
[06:55] Laura: Your calc: 60 users * 80 tokens * 5 responses / 60s = 400 tok/s, plus tokenization overhead. Micro-batching improves GPU utilization while keeping latency low. For true streaming UX we recommend micro-batching windows of ~10-30ms and tuned batch sizes. We'll calibrate in benchmark runs.
[07:17] Eric: And how do you handle KV cache for conversational flows across many concurrent sessions?
[07:22] Laura: We shard KV caches by session and keep hot prefixes in memory. For Dedicated we can allocate more memory per worker to keep larger KV caches. That reduces compute per token and improves p95s for follow-up tokens.
[07:34] (short pause)
[07:46] Customer (muffled): Are there any caveats with quantized models and streaming?
[07:50] Laura: Quantization can slightly impact generation speed depending on kernel support. Our runtime has quantization-friendly execution paths; sometimes 4-bit quantization reduces memory and increases throughput but single-token latency can vary. We'll include quantized vs fp16 p95 numbers in the benchmark.
[08:05] Maya: Great. I want to understand SLO enforcement — can we set alerts if p95 > threshold or token/sec drops below expected?
[08:12] Samir: Yes, the Console exposes alerts and you can hook into webhooks/Datadog. We also do regression alerts tied to evals and prompt sets.
[08:21] Nina: For contract and pricing — if we buy Dedicated, do you provide committed throughput guarantees?
[08:25] Samir: Dedicated comes with reserved capacity and SLA options. There are commit tiers that guarantee throughput and you get burst capacity too. We'll send the pricing + tiers.
[08:33] Eric: Ok, technical deep dive then — can Laura walk through what a tokens/sec benchmark run would look like?
[08:38] Laura: Sure. Steps: 1) Customer shares canonical prompts and sequence distribution + concurrency profile. 2) We run a load generator against a test deployment (hosted or dedicated-like infra) measuring first-token and full generation latencies, tokens/sec per GPU, GPU utilization, memory and KV cache hit rates. 3) We produce a spreadsheet with per-model, per-hardware metrics and recommend exact GPU counts / autoscale thresholds. We'll include micro-batching config used.
[09:06] Maya: How long does a benchmark take?
[09:09] Laura: Typically a day for a representative run; we do multiple runs for variance. If you want many models or large prompt sets it can take 2-3 days.
[09:16] Maya: Any limitations for streaming tests vs batch?
[09:19] Laura: Streaming tests are trickier because of network jitter and client-side buffering. We mimic a client streaming pipeline in the load test. We also test end-to-end from SDK to replicate E2E p95.
[09:29] Samir: We should also talk about regression detection. If you change model versions, our Optimize product can recommend quantization and batching changes and alert on quality regressions linked to prompt evals.
[09:40] Maya: Ok. A couple security items — KMS integration and audit logs for Private.
[09:45] Samir: We support customer-managed KMS via cloud KMS + HSM for Private. Audit logs and long-term storage options available.
[09:52] (noise)
[10:05] Nina: For the benchmark report, will you include expected monthly token costs for each topology?
[10:10] Laura: Yes we'll include rough cost modeling (tokens + infra) per topology so you can compare unit economics.
[10:17] Eric: If we run Dedicated with reserved GPUs, can we still use Hosted capacity for bursts without changing code?
[10:23] Samir: Yes, same API and routing rules can fall back to hosted or regional pools automatically.
[10:29] Maya: That seems ideal.
[10:33] (brief pause)
[10:40] Laura: Quick note on metrics we'll provide in the benchmark sheet: first-token p50/p95/p99, end-to-end p95 for 95%ile of requests, tokens/sec sustained, max observed qps, GPU util, KV cache hit rate, and memory usage.
[10:55] Maya: For p95 targets, is there an example config that reliably gives p95 < 300ms?
[10:59] Laura: Typical config: Dedicated low-latency pool, A100 or similar with fp16, micro-batching configured to 10-20ms, hot warm cache enabled, and reserved capacity to avoid multi-tenant interference. We'll verify with your prompts.
[11:15] Eric: Are there any operational gotchas — e.g., cold-starts, model loading times affecting latency when rolling?
[11:21] Laura: Model loading can add seconds on cold starts. We keep models warm in Dedicated; for rollouts we do canary deploys with warmup and traffic mirroring to avoid user-facing cold starts.
[11:33] Maya: Good. One last thing — if we need a firm SLA for p95, what does that look like legally?
[11:39] Samir: For enterprise contracts we can include SLA clauses for uptime and latency tiers tied to Dedicated commits. Exact terms depend on tier and runbook. We'll involve our legal ops once you decide to proceed.
[11:52] (wrap-up)
[12:05] Samir: Ok to recap: 1) Maya to send representative prompts and concurrency profile by 2025-03-12. 2) Samir will send pricing and contract starter by 2025-03-07. 3) Laura will run benchmark against Dedicated-like infra once prompts received and share results (tokens/sec, p95 traces) by 2025-03-10/11. 4) Schedule SE deep dive week of 2025-03-17.
[12:35] Maya: That works. Thanks everyone.
[12:40] Eric: Thanks.
[12:43] Samir: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email.

Transcript notes: occasional mistranscriptions (e.g., "KV cash" instead of KV cache in automated sections), speaker attributions sometimes generic. References to shared artifacts: pricing sheet, benchmark spreadsheet, security pack.
